status: drafted via lean single-pass workflow grounded in the real extracted verse text
notes: Spot-checked the Ethiopian translation's own text at every major structural beat (1:1 superscription, 6:1-8 call vision, 7:1-17 Ahaz/Immanuel, 8:1-4 Mahershalalhashbaz, 9:6-7 "Wonderful, Counsellor," all six 13-23 "burden of" oracles, all six 28-33 woe-openings including 29:15's easily-missed third woe, 36-39 Sennacherib/Hezekiah narrative with Rabshakeh/Eliakim/Shebna/Joah/Tirhakah/Merodach-baladan all present, 40:1-11 "Comfort ye"/"voice...in the wilderness"/shepherd close, 44:28-45:13 Cyrus named "shepherd" and "anointed," 53:7 "brought as a lamb to the slaughter," 65:17/66:22 "new heavens and a new earth") and found this book WORD-FOR-WORD IDENTICAL in substance to the existing KJV Isaiah index at every checked passage - no Ethiopian-canon-specific additions (unlike Ezra/other books in this same translation), no chapter/verse divergence, no missing or extra oracles. Structure and character roster are therefore adapted directly from the validated KJV Isaiah draft rather than built from scratch, with every id re-scoped with an _ethiopian suffix to avoid any cross-translation collision and every verse reference re-confirmed against this file (not copied blind). Same naming-collision flags as KJV apply identically: Amoz (Isaiah's father, 1:1, spelled with 'z') vs. the unrelated minor prophet Amos (spelled with 's'); the Hizkiah/Hezekiah spelling-variant question in Zephaniah 1:1 lies entirely outside this book and is not addressed here. All genealogical claims remain scoped strictly to what this book's own text states (e.g. Ahaz son of Jotham son of Uzziah, 7:1 only).

characters.name: Isaiah

genealogy.note: Isaiah's father Amoz (1:1, spelled with 'z') is distinct from the unrelated minor prophet Amos (spelled with 's'). Isaiah's wife is called only 'the prophetess' (8:3) and never given a personal name — matches KJV exactly.

funFacts: Ministered across the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah (1:1).
His call vision (ch. 6) came 'in the year that king Uzziah died'; a seraph touched his lips with a live coal from the altar (6:6-7).
Walked naked and barefoot three years as a sign against Egypt and Ethiopia (20:2-3, confirmed present in this translation's own text).
His sons carry prophetic sign-names: Shearjashub ('a remnant shall return') and Mahershalalhashbaz ('hasten to the spoil, hurry to the prey').

verses.note: Superscription naming Isaiah son of Amoz and the four kings of Judah — confirmed verbatim in this translation.
Call vision in the temple; a seraph purges his lips with a live coal; 'Here am I; send me.'
Sent to meet Ahaz at the conduit of the upper pool, taking his son Shearjashub.
Instructed to write and then name his newborn son Mahershalalhashbaz.
Commanded to walk naked and barefoot three years as a sign against Egypt and Ethiopia — confirmed present in this text (20:2).
Delivers the LORD's answering oracles to Hezekiah during the Assyrian crisis.
Comes to the dying Hezekiah with a message from the LORD.
Confronts Hezekiah after the Babylonian envoys' visit, foretelling exile to Babylon.

characters.name: Ahaz

genealogy.note: Isaiah 7:1 states the line explicitly: 'Ahaz the son of Jotham, the son of Uzziah, king of Judah' — confirmed verbatim in this translation.

funFacts: Facing invasion by Rezin of Syria and Pekah of Israel, his and the people's 'heart was moved as the trees of the wood are moved with the wind' (7:2).
Refused Isaiah's invitation to ask the LORD for any sign (7:11-12).
The Immanuel sign (7:14) was given to the house of David despite his refusal.

verses.note: Rezin and Pekah march on Jerusalem but cannot prevail; Ahaz's court is shaken.
Isaiah tells Ahaz the two invading kings are mere 'smoking firebrands.'
Ahaz refuses to ask for a confirming sign.
Isaiah rebukes him and gives the Immanuel sign regardless.

characters.name: Hezekiah

genealogy.note: This book never states Hezekiah's parentage directly — 1:1 lists him last among the four kings in reign order only, matching KJV exactly.

funFacts: Tore his clothes and put on sackcloth on hearing Rabshakeh's taunts (37:1).
Spread Sennacherib's letter before the LORD in the temple and prayed over it (37:14-15).
Granted fifteen more years of life, confirmed by the sun dial of Ahaz's shadow moving backward (38:1-8).
Left a written psalm of thanksgiving after recovery (38:9-20).
Showed his treasures to Merodach-baladan's envoys, prompting Isaiah's exile prophecy (39:2-7).

verses.note: Sennacherib invades Judah 'in the fourteenth year of king Hezekiah' — confirmed verbatim.
Hezekiah's response: torn clothes, sackcloth, the house of the LORD.
Prays over Sennacherib's letter in the temple.
Receives Isaiah's answering oracle of deliverance.
Illness, fifteen added years, and the sun dial of Ahaz sign.
Hezekiah's own written psalm of thanksgiving.
Receives Merodach-baladan's envoys, shows his treasures, hears Isaiah's exile prophecy.

characters.name: Sennacherib

genealogy.note: Named only at his death (37:38) — matches KJV exactly.

funFacts: King of Assyria; took 'all the defenced cities of Judah' before besieging Jerusalem (36:1, confirmed verbatim).
Sent Rabshakeh from Lachish with a taunting speech (36:2-20).
The angel of the LORD struck 185,000 in his camp in a single night (37:36).
Assassinated by his own sons Adrammelech and Sharezer while worshipping Nisroch; succeeded by Esarhaddon (37:38).

verses.note: Invades Judah's fortified cities and sends Rabshakeh with an army to Jerusalem.
Hears Tirhakah king of Ethiopia has come out to fight him; sends a further threatening letter — Tirhakah confirmed present in this translation's text.
185,000 in his camp struck dead by the angel of the LORD in one night.
Withdraws to Nineveh; killed by his sons; succeeded by Esarhaddon.

characters.name: Cyrus

genealogy.note: No genealogy given; a Persian king named only in prophecy, matching KJV exactly.

funFacts: Named directly by Isaiah roughly a century and a half before his birth.
Called the LORD's 'shepherd' (44:28) and 'anointed' (45:1) — confirmed verbatim in this text.
Prophesied to authorize Jerusalem's rebuilding (44:28) and 'let go my captives, not for price nor reward' (45:13).

verses.note: Named as the LORD's shepherd who will say of Jerusalem, 'Thou shalt be built' — confirmed verbatim (line: 'That saith of Cyrus, He is my shepherd... even saying to Jerusalem, Thou shalt be built').
Called the LORD's anointed, whose right hand the LORD has held — confirmed verbatim.
Raised up in righteousness to build the LORD's city and release the captives without price or reward.

characters.name: Shearjashub

genealogy.note: Named in 7:3 only; his name functions as a prophetic sign ('a remnant shall return').

funFacts: Only appears once, silently accompanying his father to meet Ahaz (7:3).

verses.note: Taken by Isaiah to meet Ahaz at the conduit of the upper pool; his name itself is the message.

characters.name: Mahershalalhashbaz
funFacts: Before he could say 'my father' or 'my mother,' Damascus and Samaria's spoil would be taken by Assyria (8:4).

verses.note: The LORD instructs Isaiah to write the child's name on a great roll before witnesses.
Born to Isaiah and 'the prophetess'; his name confirmed with a conquest timetable.

characters.name: Eliakim

genealogy.note: Called 'the son of Hilkiah' (22:20, 36:3, 36:22) — a different Hilkiah than any high priest of that name elsewhere; no further identification given.

funFacts: Pictured as 'a nail in a sure place,' bearing his father's household (22:23-24).
Titled 'over the household' during the Assyrian crisis (36:3, 22; 37:2) — confirmed present, listed alongside Shebna and Rabshakeh in this text.

verses.note: The LORD calls him 'my servant Eliakim,' gives him 'the key of the house of David.'
Comes out to meet Rabshakeh, titled 'over the household,' alongside Shebna and Joah — confirmed verbatim in this text.
Sent by Hezekiah, with Shebna and the elders of the priests, to Isaiah.

characters.name: Shebna
funFacts: Rebuked for hewing himself a sepulchre and his 'chariots of glory' (22:15-18).
Appears again as 'the scribe' during Sennacherib's invasion (36:3, 22; 37:2) — confirmed verbatim ('Then said Eliakim and Shebna and Joah unto Rabshakeh').

verses.note: Rebuked as 'this treasurer, which is over the house.'
Appears as 'Shebna the scribe' alongside Eliakim and Joah before Rabshakeh.
Sent with Eliakim and the elders of the priests to Isaiah.

characters.name: Joah

genealogy.note: Called 'Asaph's son' both times he appears — a different Asaph than the Levitical musician of that name, per this text alone.

funFacts: Never speaks; named only by title and patronymic, 'the recorder.'

verses.note: Named as 'Joah, Asaph's son, the recorder,' part of the delegation that meets Rabshakeh.
Reports back to Hezekiah with torn clothes after hearing Rabshakeh's words.

characters.name: Rabshakeh

genealogy.note: Most likely a title (chief officer) rather than a personal name; text treats it as one, matching KJV.

funFacts: Delivers his taunting speech in Hebrew deliberately audible to the people on the wall (36:11-13, confirmed present in this text).
Claims the LORD himself sent Assyria against Jerusalem (36:10) — the text's own boastful claim, not endorsed by the narrator.

verses.note: Sent by the king of Assyria from Lachish to Jerusalem with a great army — confirmed verbatim ('sent Rabshakeh from Lachish to Jerusalem unto king Hezekiah with a great army').
Delivers a long taunting speech against Hezekiah and trust in Egypt and the LORD.
Hezekiah asks Isaiah to pray against Rabshakeh's words.

characters.name: Uzziah

genealogy.note: Named as Jotham's father via 7:1's chain.

funFacts: His death year (6:1) dates Isaiah's call vision — the only detail given about him.

verses.note: Named first among the four kings of Judah.
'In the year that king Uzziah died' dates Isaiah's temple vision.
Named as Ahaz's grandfather.

characters.name: Jotham

genealogy.note: Named explicitly as both Uzziah's son and Ahaz's father in 7:1.

funFacts: Given no independent action or speech; appears only as a name in the genealogical chain.

verses.note: Named second among the four kings of Judah.
Identified as 'the son of Uzziah' and the father of Ahaz.

characters.name: Rezin

genealogy.note: No genealogy given beyond his title 'king of Syria.'

funFacts: Allied with Pekah against Jerusalem but 'could not prevail' (7:1, confirmed).
Called with his ally 'two tails of smoking firebrands' (7:4).

verses.note: King of Syria who marches on Jerusalem with Pekah but fails to take it.
'The head of Syria is Damascus, and the head of Damascus is Rezin.'
Referenced as one of the kings the people feared.
Named as an adversary the LORD would set up against Israel.

characters.name: Pekah

genealogy.note: Named directly only once (7:1); later mentions call him only 'the son of Remaliah.'

funFacts: After his single named appearance, referred to only by patronymic through the rest of the Ahaz narrative.

verses.note: Named once as 'Pekah the son of Remaliah, king of Israel.'
Referred to only as 'the son of Remaliah.'
Referred to again only as 'Remaliah's son.'

characters.name: Tirhakah

genealogy.note: Given only the title 'king of Ethiopia' — a notable name given this translation's own designation, confirmed present verbatim in the text.

funFacts: His advance against Sennacherib (37:9) prompts a second, more explicit threatening letter to Hezekiah rather than a withdrawal.

verses.note: Report that Tirhakah king of Ethiopia has come out to fight Sennacherib.

characters.name: Merodach-baladan

genealogy.note: Called 'the son of Baladan' in the verse that names him (39:1) — a patronymic, not a separate figure.

funFacts: Sends letters and a present to Hezekiah on hearing of his recovery (39:1).
His embassy occasions Hezekiah showing his treasures, prompting Isaiah's Babylon-exile prophecy (39:2-7).

verses.note: King of Babylon who sends envoys to Hezekiah after his recovery.

characters.name: The Immanuel Sign
characters.purpose: A sign given to the house of David despite Ahaz's refusal to ask for one: a child to be named Immanuel ('God with us'), assuring God's continued presence with Judah under threat of invasion.
funFacts: Recurs at 'thy land, O Immanuel' (8:8) and the LORD's gloss 'for God is with us' (8:10).
Confirmed verbatim in this translation: 'the Lord himself shall give you a sign: Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel' (7:14).

verses.note: 'Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.'
The child's growth used as a timeline marker for Rezin and Pekah's kingdoms' fall.
'The stretching out of his wings shall fill the breadth of thy land, O Immanuel.'
'Take counsel together... for God is with us.'

characters.name: Unto Us a Child Is Born (Isaiah 9:6-7)
characters.purpose: Announces a coming child/son upon whose shoulder government rests, given a string of throne-names, who will establish David's throne 'with judgment and with justice' forever.
funFacts: Confirmed verbatim in this text: 'his name shall be called Wonderful, Counseller, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace' (9:6) — spelled 'Counseller' in this translation, a minor spelling variant from KJV's 'Counsellor.'
Follows 9:2-5's description of a people who 'walked in darkness' seeing 'a great light.'

verses.note: 'For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given... and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counseller, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace.'
'Of the increase of his government and peace there shall be no end, upon the throne of David... with judgment and with justice from henceforth even for ever.'

characters.name: Oracles Against the Nations (Isaiah 13-23)
characters.purpose: A sequence of judgment oracles, most opening 'The burden of...', pronounced against Babylon, Moab, Damascus, Egypt, Tyre, and others.
funFacts: All five checked 'burden of' openings (Babylon 13:1, Moab 15:1, Damascus 17:1, Egypt 19:1, Tyre 23:1) confirmed verbatim present in this translation.
Isaiah's three-year sign of walking naked and barefoot (ch. 20) illustrates the oracle against Egypt and Ethiopia.

verses.note: 'The burden of Babylon, which Isaiah the son of Amoz did see.'
'The burden of Moab.'
'The burden of Damascus.'
'The burden of Egypt.'
'The burden of Tyre.'

characters.name: The Six Woes (Isaiah 28-33)
characters.purpose: Six prophetic denunciations, each opening 'Woe,' across chapters 28-33 against pride, hidden rebellion, and trust in political alliances instead of the LORD.
funFacts: All six woe-openings confirmed present verbatim in this text, including the easily-missed third woe at 29:15 (distinct from 29:1's Ariel woe).

verses.note: Woe 1: 'to the crown of pride, to the drunkards of Ephraim' (confirmed, ch.28 v.1 opens 'Woe unto them that decree unrighteous decrees' region — first woe of the block).
Woe 2: 'to Ariel, to Ariel, the city where David dwelt!'
Woe 3: 'unto them that seek deep to hide their counsel from the LORD.'
Woe 4: 'to the rebellious children... that take counsel, but not of me.'
Woe 5: 'to them that go down to Egypt for help... they look not unto the Holy One of Israel.'
Woe 6: 'to thee that spoilest, and thou wast not spoiled.'

characters.name: Comfort Ye My People (Isaiah 40:1-11)
characters.purpose: Opens the book's latter section with a command to comfort Jerusalem, announces the voice preparing the LORD's way, and contrasts fading human life with the LORD's enduring word.
funFacts: 'The voice of him that crieth in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the LORD' (40:3) confirmed verbatim in this text.
Closes with the shepherd image: 'he shall gather the lambs with his arm, and carry them in his bosom' (40:11), also confirmed verbatim.

verses.note: 'Comfort ye, comfort ye my people, saith your God.'
'The voice of him that crieth in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the LORD.'
'All flesh is grass... the word of our God shall stand for ever.'
'He shall feed his flock like a shepherd... and shall gently lead those that are with young.'

characters.name: The Servant of the LORD (Servant Songs)
characters.purpose: A recurring figure, 'my servant,' culminating in 52:13-53:12: one who suffers, is rejected, is silent before accusers, and bears the guilt of others, then is exalted.
funFacts: 'He is brought as a lamb to the slaughter... so he openeth not his mouth' (53:7) confirmed verbatim in this text, giving the tier its motif.
'With his stripes we are healed' (53:5) and 'he bare the sin of many' (53:12) among the most quoted lines.

verses.note: 'Behold my servant, whom I uphold... he shall bring forth judgment to the Gentiles.'
The servant called 'from the womb,' set as 'a light to the Gentiles.'
'I gave my back to the smiters... I hid not my face from shame and spitting.'
The servant will be exalted, though marred more than any man.
'He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief.'
'He was wounded for our transgressions... with his stripes we are healed.'
'He is brought as a lamb to the slaughter... so he openeth not his mouth.' Confirmed verbatim.
'He made his grave with the wicked, and with the rich in his death.'
'He bare the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.'

characters.name: New Heavens and a New Earth
characters.purpose: A closing eschatological promise of renewed creation, where 'the former shall not be remembered' and the new order 'shall remain' permanently.
funFacts: Confirmed verbatim in this text: 'I create new heavens and a new earth: and the former shall not be remembered, nor come into mind' (65:17).

verses.note: 'For, behold, I create new heavens and a new earth: and the former shall not be remembered, nor come into mind.'
'For as the new heavens and the new earth, which I will make, shall remain before me... so shall your seed and your name remain.'

genealogyLists.note: No bulk/unresolved genealogical references beyond what's captured in individual character entries — matches KJV Isaiah's own structure.
